title: Micro-organisms
prerequisites: Idea that living things are made of cells.
Knowledge that some diseases spread from one person to another.
Familiarity with a simple microscope and why it is needed.
Basic understanding that food gets spoiled if left in the open.

topics.title: Microorganisms and Their Classification
topics.quick_summary: Microorganisms are living organisms too small to be seen with the naked eye, and they are grouped into five classes — bacteria, fungi, protozoa, algae and viruses.
topics.real_life: The greenish slime on a wet wall is algae, the white fuzz on stale bread is fungus, and the curd in your kitchen is made by bacteria — three different microbes in one house.

detailed.definition: Microorganisms, or microbes, are organisms so small that they cannot be seen with the unaided eye and need a microscope to be observed.
detailed.key_idea: Microbes may be unicellular (bacteria, some algae, protozoa) or multicellular (most fungi, some algae). They live everywhere — in soil, water, air, inside our bodies, in hot springs, in ice and in deserts.
detailed.working_principle: Bacteria are classified by shape into cocci (spherical), bacilli (rod-shaped), spirilla (spiral) and vibrio (comma-shaped). Gram staining separates bacteria into Gram-positive (thick peptidoglycan wall, stain purple) and Gram-negative (thin wall, stain pink).
applications: Amoeba, Paramecium and Plasmodium are protozoa; Chlamydomonas and Spirogyra are algae.
Yeast, Penicillium, Aspergillus, Rhizopus and mushrooms are fungi.
Lichen is a symbiotic partnership of an alga and a fungus; mycorrhiza is a fungus–root partnership.

points: Five groups of microbes: bacteria, fungi, protozoa, algae and viruses.
Bacterial shapes: coccus (round), bacillus (rod), spirillum (spiral), vibrio (comma).
Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) are bacteria that photosynthesise and fix nitrogen.
Microbes are found in ice, hot springs, deserts and marshy land — everywhere.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first observed microorganisms in 1674.
mistakes: Calling cyanobacteria 'algae' — they are bacteria (prokaryotes), despite the old name blue-green algae.
Assuming all microorganisms are unicellular — many fungi and algae are multicellular.
Thinking a microscope is only needed for bacteria; almost all microbes need magnification.
topics.memory_hook: 'Ba-Fu-Pro-Al-Vi' — Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa, Algae, Viruses; and for shapes, 'Cocci are Circles, Bacilli are Bars'.
topics.advanced: Extremophiles are microbes that thrive where nothing else can — thermophiles in hot springs above 80 °C, halophiles in salt lakes. The heat-stable enzyme Taq polymerase, taken from a hot-spring bacterium, made modern DNA testing possible.

topics.title: Viruses — Living or Non-living?
topics.quick_summary: A virus is on the borderline between the living and the non-living — it reproduces only inside a living host cell and is completely inert outside it.
topics.real_life: The common cold, influenza, chickenpox, polio and COVID-19 are all caused by viruses, which is why antibiotics do not help against them.

detailed.definition: A virus is an infectious particle made of a nucleic acid core (DNA or RNA) surrounded by a protein coat called a capsid, which multiplies only inside a living host cell.
detailed.key_idea: Outside a host, a virus can be crystallised like a chemical and shows no sign of life. Inside a host cell, it hijacks the cell's machinery to make copies of itself — so it is described as an obligate intracellular parasite.
detailed.working_principle: The virus attaches to a specific host cell, injects its nucleic acid, forces the cell to manufacture viral parts, assembles new virus particles and finally bursts the cell to release them.
applications: Bacteriophages are viruses that attack bacteria and are used in phage therapy.
Vaccines use weakened or inactivated viruses to train the immune system.
Viral diseases in humans: polio, measles, chickenpox, mumps, influenza, AIDS, dengue.

points: Virus = nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) + protein coat; never both DNA and RNA.
Living characteristic: it reproduces and has genetic material.
Non-living characteristics: it can be crystallised, has no cell structure and no metabolism of its own.
Antibiotics do NOT work against viruses — only vaccines and antiviral drugs help.
Viruses are much smaller than bacteria and are seen only with an electron microscope.
mistakes: Taking antibiotics for a cold or flu — these are viral and antibiotics have no effect.
Saying a virus contains both DNA and RNA; it contains only one of the two.
Calling viruses cells — they have no cell membrane, cytoplasm or organelles.
topics.memory_hook: 'A virus is a pirate ship — dead in the harbour, deadly once it boards a living cell.'
topics.advanced: Some viruses insert their genes permanently into the host chromosome; about 8% of the human genome is made of such ancient viral sequences, and a few of them now perform useful functions such as helping form the placenta.

topics.title: Useful Microorganisms
topics.quick_summary: Microbes are used to make curd, bread and alcohol, to produce antibiotics and vaccines, to clean up the environment and to increase soil fertility.
topics.real_life: The bubbles in a rising dough, the sourness of curd, and the penicillin in a prescription are all the work of useful microorganisms.

detailed.definition: Useful microorganisms are microbes whose activities benefit humans — in food production, medicine, agriculture and waste management.
detailed.key_idea: The single most important microbial process for humans is fermentation — the breakdown of sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide (or into acid) in the absence of oxygen, discovered by Louis Pasteur in 1857.
detailed.working_principle: Lactobacillus converts milk sugar to lactic acid, curdling milk into curd. Yeast (Saccharomyces) ferments sugar to alcohol and CO₂, making bread rise and producing wine and beer. Soil bacteria decompose dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.
applications: Antibiotics: penicillin from the fungus Penicillium (Alexander Fleming, 1929), streptomycin, tetracycline, erythromycin.
Vaccines against cholera, tuberculosis, smallpox and hepatitis (Edward Jenner, smallpox, 1798).
Rhizobium in legume root nodules and Azotobacter in soil fix atmospheric nitrogen; blue-green algae act as biofertilizers in paddy fields.

points: Lactobacillus → curd; Yeast → bread, wine, beer (fermentation).
Penicillin was the first antibiotic, discovered by Alexander Fleming from Penicillium.
A vaccine contains dead or weakened microbes that make the body produce antibodies.
Rhizobium lives in root nodules of leguminous plants and fixes nitrogen.
Decomposers convert dead plant and animal remains into humus.
mistakes: Saying yeast makes curd — curd is made by Lactobacillus; yeast makes bread and alcohol.
Confusing antibiotic with vaccine: an antibiotic kills bacteria already inside you, a vaccine prevents the disease beforehand.
Taking antibiotics without completing the prescribed course, which breeds resistant bacteria.
topics.memory_hook: 'Lacto for Lassi, Yeast for Yeast-bread' — and 'Fleming Found Fungus's Penicillin'.
topics.advanced: Antibiotic resistance arises by natural selection: a few bacteria carrying a resistance gene survive treatment and multiply. This is why doctors insist on finishing the full course — stopping early leaves behind exactly the toughest survivors.

topics.title: Harmful Microorganisms and Food Preservation
topics.quick_summary: Pathogens cause communicable diseases in humans, animals and plants, and spoil food — which is why food is preserved by heat, cold, chemicals, drying or salting.
topics.real_life: Milk in a sealed tetra pack lasts for months because it has been pasteurised, and pickles keep for a year because oil and salt keep microbes out.

detailed.definition: Disease-causing microorganisms are called pathogens; a disease that spreads from an infected person to a healthy person is a communicable disease. Food preservation is the treatment of food to prevent microbial spoilage.
detailed.key_idea: Pathogens spread through air (cough, sneeze), water (contaminated drinking water), food, direct contact, and through carriers — animals such as the female Anopheles mosquito (malaria), the Aedes mosquito (dengue) and the housefly.
detailed.working_principle: Preservation works by removing what microbes need: heat kills them (pasteurisation, boiling, canning), cold slows them (refrigeration, freezing), drying and salting remove water, and chemical preservatives, sugar and oil make the food unsuitable for growth.
applications: Human diseases: tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid (bacteria); malaria, kala-azar (protozoa); polio, chickenpox, influenza (viruses).
Plant diseases: citrus canker (bacteria), rust of wheat (fungi), yellow vein mosaic of bhindi (virus).
Preservatives: sodium benzoate and sodium metabisulphite in jams, squashes and sauces.

points: Pasteurisation: milk heated to about 70 °C for 15–30 seconds, then chilled suddenly.
Female Anopheles mosquito carries the malarial parasite Plasmodium.
Salt and sugar preserve food by drawing water out of microbial cells (osmosis).
Common preservatives: sodium benzoate, sodium metabisulphite; oil and vinegar in pickles.
Some fungi produce toxins; food poisoning is caused by eating food spoiled by microbes.
mistakes: Thinking pasteurisation sterilises milk completely — it only kills most microbes, so milk must still be refrigerated.
Confusing the vector with the pathogen: the mosquito is the carrier, Plasmodium is the pathogen.
Believing refrigeration kills microorganisms — it only slows their growth down.
topics.memory_hook: 'Pasteur Pasteurises' — and to preserve, 'Too Hot, Too Cold, Too Dry or Too Salty for a microbe to live'.
topics.advanced: The nitrogen cycle links harmful and helpful microbes: nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert N₂ to nitrates, nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonia, and denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen to the atmosphere — keeping the atmospheric level of nitrogen roughly constant at 78%.
